title: Das Meerhäschen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 191. Text from Wikisource („Das Meerhäschen (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: A princess who can see her whole kingdom from a tower of twelve windows challenges every suitor to hide from her three times or lose his head; ninety-seven have already failed when a young man wins the help of a raven, a fish, and a fox. For his third and best hiding place he is transformed into a small creature called a Meerhäschen, literally a “little-sea-hare,” sold to the princess as a curiosity — the exact real-world animal the Grimms had in mind is not settled, and the name is left untranslated in the title for that reason.

sentences.t: Es war einmal eine Königstochter, die hatte in ihrem Schloß hoch unter der Zinne einen Saal mit zwölf Fenstern, die giengen nach allen Himmelsgegenden,
sentences.l: There was once a king’s-daughter, she had in her castle high up under the battlement a hall with twelve windows, they looked toward all quarters of the sky,
sentences.i: There was once a king’s daughter who had in her castle, high up beneath the battlements, a hall with twelve windows that looked out to every quarter of the sky,
sentences.n: “die hatte” is a demonstrative, not a relative: the German starts a fresh statement — she had — the way a story told aloud does, and “die giengen” does the same again for the windows. gehen said of a window is to face, to look out. Die Zinne is the crenellated top of a wall or tower.

sentences.t: und wenn sie hinaufstieg und umher schaute, so konnte sie ihr ganzes Reich übersehen.
sentences.l: and when she climbed up and looked about, then could she survey her whole realm.
sentences.i: and when she climbed up and looked about her, she could survey her whole realm.
sentences.n: übersehen here is to look over, to take in at one glance; the modern sense to overlook, to miss, came later. The so at the head of the main clause after a when-clause is a resumptive marker German likes and English does not need.

sentences.t: Aus dem ersten sah sie schon schärfer als andere Menschen, in dem zweiten noch besser, in dem dritten noch deutlicher und so immer weiter bis in dem zwölften, wo sie alles sah, was über und unter der Erde war und ihr nichts verborgen bleiben konnte.
sentences.l: Out of the first she saw already more sharply than other people, in the second still better, in the third still more distinctly and so ever further until in the twelfth, where she saw everything that was above and under the earth and nothing could remain hidden to her.
sentences.i: From the first she already saw more sharply than other people; from the second better still; from the third more distinctly again, and so on and on up to the twelfth, where she saw everything that was above the earth and beneath it, and nothing could stay hidden from her.
sentences.n: The tale counts its way up the twelve windows here, and will count its way up them twice more before it ends; the number is not decoration, since the youngest brother has to get past all twelve. noch with a comparative means still, yet — noch besser, better still.

sentences.t: Weil sie aber stolz war, sich niemand unterwerfen wollte und die Herrschaft allein behalten, so ließ sie bekannt machen, es sollte niemand ihr Gemahl werden, der sich nicht so vor ihr verstecken könnte daß es ihr unmöglich wäre ihn zu finden.
sentences.l: But because she was proud, wanted to subject herself to nobody and to keep the rule alone, she had it made known, nobody should become her husband who could not hide himself before her so that it would be impossible for her to find him.
sentences.i: But because she was proud, and would submit to nobody, and meant to keep the rule to herself, she had it proclaimed that no one should become her husband unless he could hide from her so well that she could not possibly find him.
sentences.n: die Herrschaft here is rule, dominion — not the gentry, which the same word can also mean. “ließ … bekannt machen” is lassen with an infinitive: had a thing made known. From there on everything stands in the subjunctive of reported speech — sollte, könnte, wäre — which is how German marks these as her terms rather than the teller’s.

sentences.t: Wer es aber versuche und sie entdecke ihn, so werde ihm das Haupt abgeschlagen und auf einen Pfahl gesteckt.
sentences.l: Whoever however should attempt it and she discover him, then would his head be struck off and stuck on a stake.
sentences.i: But whoever should attempt it — if she discovered him, his head would be struck off and set on a stake.
sentences.n: versuche, entdecke and werde are all subjunctive, so the proclamation goes on speaking in her voice. das Haupt is the elevated word for head, and this tale keeps it for the heads on the stakes. The sentence changes course in the middle — it begins “whoever attempts it” and ends as a plain conditional — and the German leaves the join unrepaired.

sentences.t: Es standen schon sieben und neunzig Pfähle mit todten Häuptern vor dem Schloß, und in langer Zeit meldete sich niemand.
sentences.l: There stood already seven and ninety stakes with dead heads before the castle, and in a long time nobody announced himself.
sentences.i: Ninety-seven stakes already stood before the castle with dead heads on them, and for a long while nobody came forward.
sentences.n: German counts the units before the tens — sieben und neunzig, seven-and-ninety — as English once did in four-and-twenty. todten is the 1857 spelling of toten. “sich melden” is to present oneself, to come forward.

sentences.t: Die Königstochter war vergnügt und dachte „ich werde nun für mein Lebtag frei bleiben.“
sentences.l: The king’s-daughter was content and thought “I shall now for my life-day remain free.”
sentences.i: The king’s daughter was well pleased and thought: “Now I shall stay free for the rest of my days.”
sentences.n: “für mein Lebtag” is an old fixed phrase — for my lifetime, for as long as I live — and keeps the singular Tag where the sense is plural. The tale prints her thoughts inside quotation marks exactly as it prints her speech, and does so for every character in turn.

sentences.t: Da erschienen drei Brüder vor ihr und kündigten ihr an daß sie ihr Glück versuchen wollten.
sentences.l: Then appeared three brothers before her and announced to her that they wanted to try their fortune.
sentences.i: Then three brothers appeared before her and announced that they meant to try their luck.
sentences.n: ankündigen is separable and drops its particle an at the end of the clause: “kündigten … an”. “sein Glück versuchen” is the standing phrase for trying one’s luck, and three brothers trying it in turn is the shape a great many tales in this book take.

sentences.t: Der älteste glaubte sicher zu sein, wenn er in ein Kalkloch krieche, aber sie erblickte ihn schon aus dem ersten Fenster, ließ ihn herausziehen und ihm das Haupt abschlagen.
sentences.l: The eldest believed to be safe if he crept into a lime-pit, but she caught sight of him already from the first window, had him pulled out and his head struck off.
sentences.i: The eldest thought he would be safe if he crept into a lime-pit, but she caught sight of him from the very first window, had him dragged out and his head struck off.
sentences.n: krieche is subjunctive because the plan is reported rather than narrated. “ließ ihn herausziehen” — lassen does the work English does with have: had him pulled out. A Kalkloch is the pit in which lime was slaked, a hole in the ground beside a building site.

sentences.t: Der zweite kroch in den Keller des Schlosses, aber auch diesen erblickte sie aus dem ersten Fenster, und es war um ihn geschehen: sein Haupt kam auf den neun und neunzigsten Pfahl.
sentences.l: The second crept into the cellar of the castle, but this one too she caught sight of from the first window, and it was done for about him: his head came onto the nine-and-ninetieth stake.
sentences.i: The second crept into the castle cellar, but she caught sight of him too from the first window, and it was all over with him: his head went onto the ninety-ninth stake.
sentences.n: “es ist um ihn geschehen” is the fixed phrase — it is all over with him, he is done for. “auch diesen” is fronted for emphasis, so the verb comes next and the subject after it. The count is exact: ninety-seven stood there, the eldest brother made the ninety-eighth, this is the ninety-ninth, and the hundredth is left waiting.

sentences.t: Da trat der jüngste vor sie hin und bat sie möchte ihm einen Tag Bedenkzeit geben, auch so gnädig sein es ihm zweimal zu schenken, wenn sie ihn entdecke:
sentences.l: Then stepped the youngest before her and begged she might give him one day of thinking-time, also be so gracious as to remit it to him twice, if she discovered him:
sentences.i: Then the youngest stepped before her and begged that she would give him a day to think it over, and be so gracious as to let him off twice if she found him:
sentences.n: hintreten is separable and hin arrives at the end: “trat … vor sie hin”. bat introduces reported speech with no daß at all, and möchte carries the request. “es ihm schenken” is to make a person a present of a thing, and so to let him off the penalty.

sentences.t: mislinge es ihm zum drittenmal, so wolle er sich nichts mehr aus seinem Leben machen.
sentences.l: should it fail him for the third time, then would he make nothing more of his life.
sentences.i: and if he failed the third time, he would set no more store by his life.
sentences.n: mislinge is a conditional clause with no wenn: German can put the verb first and mean “if …”. mislingen, the 1857 spelling of misslingen, takes the dative of the person it fails. “sich nichts aus etwas machen” is to care nothing for a thing.

sentences.t: Weil er so schön war und so herzlich bat, so sagte sie „ja, ich will dir das bewilligen, aber es wird dir nicht glücken.“
sentences.l: Because he was so handsome and begged so heartily, she said “yes, I will grant you that, but it will not succeed for you.”
sentences.i: Because he was so handsome and begged so warmly, she said: “Yes, I will grant you that — but you will not succeed.”
sentences.n: glücken takes the dative of the person a thing goes well for: “es wird dir nicht glücken”, it will not come off for you. dir is you: the princess and the youth address each other with du from their first exchange onward.

sentences.t: Den folgenden Tag sann er lange nach wie er sich verstecken wollte, aber es war vergeblich.
sentences.l: The following day he thought long after how he wanted to hide himself, but it was in vain.
sentences.i: The next day he pondered long over how he might hide himself, but it was in vain.
sentences.n: “Den folgenden Tag” is a bare accusative of time — German needs no preposition. nachsinnen is separable and nach waits at the end: “sann … nach”, pondered, mused over.

sentences.t: Da ergriff er seine Büchse und gieng hinaus auf die Jagd.
sentences.l: Then he seized his gun and went out to the hunt.
sentences.i: So he took up his gun and went out hunting.
sentences.n: Die Büchse is a rifle or fowling-piece. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging; the ie of gieng, fieng and hieng is one of this book’s constant marks and means nothing more than a long i.

sentences.t: Er sah einen Raben und nahm ihn aufs Korn; eben wollte er losdrücken, da rief der Rabe „schieß nicht, ich will dirs vergelten!“
sentences.l: He saw a raven and took him onto the bead; just then he wanted to press off, when the raven called “do not shoot, I will repay it to you!”
sentences.i: He saw a raven and took aim at it; he was just about to pull the trigger when the raven cried: “Do not shoot — I will repay you for it!”
sentences.n: “jemanden aufs Korn nehmen” is to draw a bead on a thing: das Korn is the little foresight on a gun barrel, not grain here. losdrücken is to press the trigger. dirs is dir and es run together, it to you — the small pronoun es attaches to whatever stands in front of it.

sentences.t: Er setzte ab, gieng weiter und kam an einen See, wo er einen großen Fisch überraschte, der aus der Tiefe herauf an die Oberfläche des Wassers gekommen war.
sentences.l: He set [the gun] down, went further and came to a lake, where he surprised a great fish that had come up out of the deep to the surface of the water.
sentences.i: He lowered the gun, went on, and came to a lake, where he came upon a great fish that had risen from the deep to the surface of the water.
sentences.n: absetzen said of a gun is to take it down from the shoulder — the opposite of anlegen a few lines further on. der See, masculine, is a lake; die See, feminine, is the sea, and only the article tells them apart. die Tiefe is a noun built straight from the adjective tief: the deep. The gun is supplied in square brackets in the literal line: the German says only “setzte ab”, with nothing for it to act on.

sentences.t: Als er angelegt hatte, rief der Fisch „schieß nicht, ich will dirs vergelten!“
sentences.l: When he had levelled, the fish called “do not shoot, I will repay it to you!”
sentences.i: When he had taken aim, the fish cried: “Do not shoot — I will repay you for it!”
sentences.n: anlegen said of a gun is to bring it up and sight along it. The fish repeats the raven’s words exactly, and the fox will repeat them a third time: the tale is laying its debts out in a row so that it can call them in later in the same order.

sentences.t: Er ließ ihn untertauchen, gieng weiter und begegnete einem Fuchs der hinkte.
sentences.l: He let it dive under, went further and met a fox that limped.
sentences.i: He let it dive under, went on, and met a fox that was limping.
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative — einem Fuchs — where English has a plain object: met a fox. The relative clause “der hinkte” stands with no comma before it, as the 1857 printing often prints them.

sentences.t: Er schoß und verfehlte ihn, da rief der Fuchs „komm lieber her und zieh mir den Dorn aus dem Fuß.“
sentences.l: He shot and missed him, then the fox called “come rather here and pull me the thorn out of the foot.”
sentences.i: He shot and missed, and the fox called: “Better come here and pull the thorn out of my foot.”
sentences.n: “zieh mir den Dorn aus dem Fuß” is the dative of possession: pull the thorn out of the foot to me, where English says my foot. lieber is the comparative of gern and means rather, better. komm and zieh are imperatives.

sentences.t: Er that es zwar, wollte aber dann den Fuchs tödten und ihm den Balg abziehen.
sentences.l: He did it indeed, but wanted then to kill the fox and pull the skin off him.
sentences.i: He did it, to be sure, but then he meant to kill the fox and strip off its pelt.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun, modern tun. Der Balg is the whole skin of a fur animal, taken off in one piece. “zwar … aber” admits a thing and then objects to it.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs sprach „laß ab, ich will dirs vergelten!“
sentences.l: The fox spoke “leave off, I will repay it to you!”
sentences.i: The fox said: “Leave off — I will repay you for it!”
sentences.n: ablassen is separable and here in the imperative, laß ab — leave off, let be. The third promise closes the set, and from here the tale spends them one by one in the order they were made.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling ließ ihn laufen, und da es Abend war, kehrte er heim.
sentences.l: The youth let him run, and since it was evening, he turned home.
sentences.i: The youth let it go, and as it was evening he turned homewards.
sentences.n: “laufen lassen” is to let a creature go. da at the head of a clause can be then or since; the verb at the end — war — shows this one is subordinate, so it is since. heimkehren is separable and its particle heim stands at the close.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag sollte er sich verkriechen, aber wie er sich auch den Kopf darüber zerbrach, er wußte nicht wohin.
sentences.l: On the next day he was to creep away and hide, but however he broke his head over it, he knew not whither.
sentences.i: The next day he was to hide himself away, but however he racked his brains over it, he did not know where.
sentences.n: “sich den Kopf zerbrechen” is to rack one’s brains, literally to break one’s head. “wie … auch” is the concessive: however much. wohin is a single word for to where.

sentences.t: Er gieng in den Wald zu dem Raben und sprach „ich habe dich leben lassen, jetzt sage mir wohin ich mich verkriechen soll, damit mich die Königstochter nicht sieht.“
sentences.l: He went into the wood to the raven and spoke “I have let you live, now tell me where I am to creep away, so that the king’s-daughter does not see me.”
sentences.i: He went into the wood to the raven and said: “I let you live; now tell me where I am to hide, so that the king’s daughter does not see me.”
sentences.n: “leben lassen” is lassen with a bare infinitive, to let live; in the perfect German keeps that infinitive rather than a participle — “habe … lassen”. He will say these same words to the fish and then to the fox, in the order in which the promises were made to him.

sentences.t: Der Rabe senkte den Kopf und bedachte sich lange.
sentences.l: The raven sank the head and bethought himself long.
sentences.i: The raven lowered its head and thought for a long while.
sentences.n: “sich bedenken” is to think a matter over, to take counsel with oneself. senken is the causative of sinken — to make a thing sink, to lower it.

sentences.t: Endlich schnarrte er „ich habs heraus!“
sentences.l: At last he rasped “I have it out!”
sentences.i: At last it croaked: “I have it!”
sentences.n: “etwas heraushaben” is to have worked a thing out, to have got it. habs is habe es with the pronoun swallowed into the verb. schnarren is a harsh rattling noise, the right verb for a raven; the fish and the fox each get a verb of their own.

sentences.t: Er holte ein Ei aus seinem Nest, zerlegte es in zwei Theile und schloß den Jüngling hinein: dann machte er es wieder ganz und setzte sich darauf.
sentences.l: He fetched an egg out of his nest, took it apart into two pieces and shut the youth inside: then he made it whole again and set himself on it.
sentences.i: It fetched an egg from its nest, took it apart into two halves and shut the youth inside; then it made the egg whole again and settled itself on top.
sentences.n: das Ei is the egg — the same two letters are elsewhere in this book the mild interjection ei, well now. zerlegen is to take apart into pieces, and Theile is the 1857 spelling of Teile. hineinschließen is separable and hinein goes to the end. Nothing explains how a grown man fits inside an egg, and the tale does not pause to try.

sentences.t: Als die Königstochter an das erste Fenster trat, konnte sie ihn nicht entdecken, auch nicht in den folgenden, und es fieng an ihr bange zu werden, doch im elften erblickte sie ihn.
sentences.l: When the king’s-daughter stepped to the first window, she could not discover him, nor in the following ones either, and it began to become anxious to her, but in the eleventh she caught sight of him.
sentences.i: When the king’s daughter stepped to the first window she could not find him, nor in the ones that followed, and she began to grow uneasy — but at the eleventh she caught sight of him.
sentences.n: “es wird mir bange” puts the person in the dative: the fear comes over her rather than being something she does. anfangen is separable — “fieng … an” — and fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. The count matters: eleven windows this time, where his brothers cost her only one.

sentences.t: Sie ließ den Raben schießen, das Ei holen und zerbrechen, und der Jüngling mußte heraus kommen.
sentences.l: She had the raven shot, the egg fetched and broken, and the youth had to come out.
sentences.n: One lassen governs three infinitives in a row — shot, fetched, broken — and German needs no repetition of the verb. The raven pays for its help with its life, and the tale reports it in the same breath as the rest, without comment.

sentences.t: Sie sprach „einmal ist es dir geschenkt, wenn du es nicht besser machst, so bist du verloren.“
sentences.l: She spoke “once it is remitted to you, if you do not do it better, then you are lost.”
sentences.i: She said: “Once you are let off; if you do not manage better, you are lost.”
sentences.n: “geschenkt sein” picks up the youth’s own word from his bargain — she is making him a present of the first failure. “so bist du verloren” uses the plain present for a certain future, exactly as English does in you are lost.

sentences.t: Am folgenden Tag gieng er an den See, rief den Fisch herbei und sprach „ich habe dich leben lassen, nun sage wohin soll ich mich verbergen, damit mich die Königstochter nicht sieht.“
sentences.l: On the following day he went to the lake, called the fish hither and spoke “I have let you live, now say where shall I hide myself, so that the king’s-daughter does not see me.”
sentences.i: The next day he went to the lake, called the fish to him and said: “I let you live; now say where I am to hide myself, so that the king’s daughter does not see me.”
sentences.n: herbeirufen is separable and herbei goes to the end. “wohin soll ich mich verbergen” keeps the word order of a direct question inside a reported one, which the 1857 language does freely. The words are the raven’s speech again, altered by a syllable — the repetition is the shape of the tale.

sentences.t: Der Fisch besann sich, endlich rief er „ich habs heraus! ich will dich in meinen Bauch verschließen.“
sentences.l: The fish bethought itself, at last it called “I have it out! I will shut you inside my belly.”
sentences.i: The fish thought a while, and at last it cried: “I have it! I will shut you up inside my belly.”
sentences.n: “sich besinnen” is to reflect, to cast about in one’s mind — the fish’s equivalent of the raven’s long lowering of the head. The exclamation is word for word the raven’s.

sentences.t: Er verschluckte ihn und fuhr hinab auf den Grund des Sees.
sentences.l: It swallowed him down and went down to the bottom of the lake.
sentences.i: It swallowed him down and made off to the bottom of the lake.
sentences.n: fahren need not mean to drive: it is any swift movement, and here it is a plunge. Sees is the genitive of der See, the lake.

sentences.t: Die Königstochter blickte durch ihre Fenster, auch im elften sah sie ihn nicht, und war bestürzt, doch endlich im zwölften entdeckte sie ihn.
sentences.l: The king’s-daughter looked through her windows, in the eleventh too she did not see him, and was dismayed, but at last in the twelfth she discovered him.
sentences.i: The king’s daughter looked through her windows; even at the eleventh she did not see him, and she was dismayed — but at last, at the twelfth, she found him.
sentences.n: The count climbs one window each time: the first for the two elder brothers, then the eleventh, now the twelfth and last. There is nothing above the twelfth, which is what makes the third day’s hiding the whole of the tale.

sentences.t: Sie ließ den Fisch fangen und tödten, und der Jüngling kam zum Vorschein.
sentences.l: She had the fish caught and killed, and the youth came to light.
sentences.n: “zum Vorschein kommen” is to come to light, to appear. tödten is the 1857 spelling of töten. The second helper dies as the first did, and the tale keeps its accounts without a word of regret.

sentences.t: Es kann sich jeder denken wie ihm zu Muth war.
sentences.l: Anyone can think for himself how it was with his spirits.
sentences.i: Anyone can imagine how he felt.
sentences.n: “wie einem zu Muth ist” is the standing phrase for how a person feels inside; Muth is the 1857 spelling of Mut, and here it is mood and spirits, not courage. The teller turns to the reader for a moment rather than describe the youth at all.

sentences.t: Sie sprach „Zweimal ist dirs geschenkt, aber dein Haupt wird wohl auf den hundertsten Pfahl kommen.“
sentences.l: She spoke “Twice it is remitted to you, but your head will probably come onto the hundredth stake.”
sentences.i: She said: “Twice you are let off — but your head will be going onto the hundredth stake, I fancy.”
sentences.n: wohl softens a statement into an expectation: it will come to that, I expect. The hundredth stake has stood empty since the ninety-ninth was filled, and she names it now.

sentences.t: An dem letzten Tag gieng er mit schwerem Herzen aufs Feld und begegnete dem Fuchs.
sentences.l: On the last day he went with heavy heart out to the field and met the fox.
sentences.i: On the last day he went out to the field with a heavy heart, and met the fox.
sentences.n: “mit schwerem Herzen” takes no article, as such phrases of manner do not in German. aufs is auf das run together, one of the contractions this book prints everywhere.

sentences.t: „Du weißt alle Schlupfwinkel zu finden,“ sprach er, „ich habe dich leben lassen, jetzt rath mir wohin ich mich verstecken soll, damit mich die Königstochter nicht findet.“
sentences.l: “You know all hiding-holes to find,” spoke he, “I have let you live, now advise me where I am to hide myself, so that the king’s-daughter does not find me.”
sentences.i: “You know how to find every hiding-hole,” he said. “I let you live; now advise me where I am to hide, so that the king’s daughter does not find me.”
sentences.n: “wissen zu” with an infinitive is to know how to do a thing. Ein Schlupfwinkel is a slipping-corner, a bolt-hole. rath is the imperative of rathen, modern raten, to advise; the th is this book’s spelling and nothing more.

sentences.t: „Ein schweres Stück,“ antwortete der Fuchs, und machte ein bedenkliches Gesicht.
sentences.l: “A hard piece,” answered the fox, and made a doubtful face.
sentences.i: “A hard piece of work,” answered the fox, and pulled a doubtful face.
sentences.n: schwer here is difficult, not heavy — one German word carries both, and the sentence has to decide. “ein Gesicht machen” is to pull a face; bedenklich is the look of somebody who has misgivings.

sentences.t: Endlich rief er „ich habs heraus!“
sentences.l: At last he called “I have it out!”
sentences.i: At last it cried: “I have it!”
sentences.n: The third helper says exactly what the first two said. In this tale a promise is kept in the same words it was made in, and the third time is the one that holds.

sentences.t: Er gieng mit ihm zu einer Quelle, tauchte sich hinein und kam als ein Marktkrämer und Thierhändler heraus.
sentences.l: He went with him to a spring, dipped himself in and came out as a market-pedlar and animal-dealer.
sentences.i: It went with him to a spring, dipped itself in, and came out as a market pedlar and dealer in animals.
sentences.n: hineintauchen and herauskommen both split, and their particles hinein and heraus stand at the end. hin- points away from the speaker and her- toward: in and out. Thier is the 1857 spelling of Tier.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling mußte sich auch in das Wasser tauchen, und ward in ein kleines Meerhäschen verwandelt.
sentences.l: The youth had to dip himself into the water too, and was changed into a little sea-hare.
sentences.n: Meerhäschen is a diminutive of Meerhase, sea-hare, and what animal the 1857 text has in mind is not settled. The name has been used for a sea slug, for a kind of fish, and for the guinea pig, which reached Europe by sea and was shown as a curiosity at markets; the tale itself asks only for a small tame creature a merchant can carry about and a lady can buy. ward is the old form of wurde.

sentences.t: Der Kaufmann zog in die Stadt und zeigte das artige Thierchen.
sentences.l: The merchant moved into the town and showed the pretty little animal.
sentences.i: The merchant went into the town and showed off the pretty little creature.
sentences.n: artig here is pretty, dainty, well made; the modern sense well-behaved narrowed later. Thierchen is a diminutive of Thier and marks the creature as small and taking.

sentences.t: Es lief viel Volk zusammen um es anzusehen.
sentences.l: There ran much folk together in order to look at it.
sentences.i: A great crowd ran together to look at it.
sentences.n: “viel Volk” is a great many people, and the verb stays singular with it. zusammenlaufen is separable and zusammen closes the clause. “um … anzusehen” is the purpose construction, with the zu slipped inside the separable verb: anzusehen.

sentences.t: Zuletzt kam auch die Königstochter, und weil sie großen Gefallen daran hatte, kaufte sie es und gab dem Kaufmann viel Geld dafür.
sentences.l: At last the king’s-daughter came too, and because she had great pleasure in it, she bought it and gave the merchant much money for it.
sentences.i: At last the king’s daughter came too, and because she took a great liking to it, she bought it and gave the merchant a great deal of money for it.
sentences.n: “Gefallen an etwas haben” is to take a liking to a thing; das Gefallen here is a noun, pleasure, and not the participle of fallen. daran and dafür each gather a preposition and a pronoun into one word — in it, for it.

sentences.t: Bevor er es ihr hinreichte, sagte er zu ihm „wenn die Königstochter ans Fenster geht, so krieche schnell unter ihren Zopf.“
sentences.l: Before he handed it to her, he said to it “when the king’s-daughter goes to the window, then creep quickly under her plait.”
sentences.i: Before he handed it over to her, he said to it: “When the king’s daughter goes to the window, creep quickly under her plait.”
sentences.n: ihr is the princess and ihm the little creature: German tells them apart by gender, since Meerhäschen is neuter. krieche is an imperative here. Der Zopf is the heavy plait of hair worn down the back, and a small animal could lie in it unseen.

sentences.t: Nun kam die Zeit, wo sie ihn suchen sollte.
sentences.l: Now came the time when she was to seek him.
sentences.i: Now came the time when she was to look for him.
sentences.n: wo does duty for when after a word of time, which the 1857 language allows freely and modern German still does in speech.

sentences.t: Sie trat nach der Reihe an die Fenster vom ersten bis zum elften und sah ihn nicht.
sentences.l: She stepped in turn to the windows from the first to the eleventh and did not see him.
sentences.n: “nach der Reihe” is in turn, one after another. The count is being run for the last time, and the tale walks all eleven windows through in a single line so as to leave the twelfth standing alone.

sentences.t: Als sie ihn auch bei dem zwölften nicht sah, war sie voll Angst und Zorn und schlug es so gewaltig zu, daß das Glas in allen Fenstern in tausend Stücke zersprang und das ganze Schloß erzitterte.
sentences.l: When she did not see him at the twelfth either, she was full of fear and rage and slammed it to so mightily that the glass in all the windows burst into a thousand pieces and the whole castle trembled.
sentences.i: When she did not see him at the twelfth either, she was full of fear and rage, and slammed it to so violently that the glass in every window burst into a thousand pieces and the whole castle shook.
sentences.n: zuschlagen is separable and zu closes the clause: “schlug es … zu”. The es is the twelfth window. Twelve windows have been counted up three times over, and the tale ends the counting by breaking every one of them.

sentences.t: Sie gieng zurück und fühlte das Meerhäschen unter ihrem Zopf, da packte sie es, warf es zu Boden und rief „fort mir aus den Augen!“
sentences.l: She went back and felt the sea-hare under her plait, then she seized it, threw it to the ground and cried “away from my eyes!”
sentences.i: She went back and felt the sea-hare under her plait; then she seized it, threw it to the ground and cried: “Out of my sight!”
sentences.n: “fort mir aus den Augen” has no verb at all — an order of pure impatience, with mir in the dative marking whose eyes. She has lost and does not yet know it: she is throwing away the very thing she was looking for.

sentences.t: Es lief zum Kaufmann und beide eilten zur Quelle, wo sie sich untertauchten und ihre wahre Gestalt zurück erhielten.
sentences.l: It ran to the merchant and both hurried to the spring, where they dipped themselves under and got their true shape back.
sentences.i: It ran to the merchant, and the two of them hurried to the spring, where they dipped themselves under and received their true shape again.
sentences.n: “zurück erhalten” is printed as two words in 1857 where modern German writes zurückerhalten; this book separates such compounds constantly. wahr is true in the sense of real, actual — their own shape as against the borrowed one.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling dankte dem Fuchs und sprach „der Rabe und der Fisch sind blitzdumm gegen dich, du weißt die rechten Pfiffe, das muß wahr sein!“
sentences.l: The youth thanked the fox and spoke “the raven and the fish are lightning-stupid against you, you know the right tricks, that must be true!”
sentences.i: The youth thanked the fox and said: “The raven and the fish are utter fools beside you — you know the right tricks, that must be granted!”
sentences.n: blitzdumm puts Blitz, lightning, in front of an adjective purely to intensify it, the way English says blazing or thundering. gegen dich here is compared with you. Der Pfiff is a whistle and, by transfer, a trick or a dodge. danken takes the dative — dem Fuchs.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling gieng geradezu in das Schloß.
sentences.l: The youth went straight into the castle.
sentences.n: geradezu is straight, directly, without turning aside; the word later came to mean downright, which is the only sense left in modern German.

sentences.t: Die Königstochter wartete schon auf ihn und fügte sich ihrem Schicksal.
sentences.l: The king’s-daughter was already waiting for him and submitted herself to her fate.
sentences.i: The king’s daughter was already waiting for him, and submitted to her fate.
sentences.n: “sich fügen” takes the dative of whatever one yields to. The tale gives her no speech here at all: the whole of her defeat is one verb.

sentences.t: Die Hochzeit ward gefeiert und er war jetzt der König und Herr des ganzen Reichs.
sentences.l: The wedding was celebrated and he was now the king and lord of the whole realm.
sentences.n: ward is the old passive auxiliary, wurde in modern German. Reichs is the genitive with -s. The proud princess who meant to keep the rule to herself loses it in a single sentence, and the tale spends no more words on it than that.

sentences.t: Er erzählte ihr niemals wohin er sich zum drittenmal versteckt und wer ihm geholfen hatte,
sentences.l: He never told her where he had hidden himself the third time and who had helped him,
sentences.n: The auxiliary hatte serves both clauses at once and is written only in the second — “versteckt und wer ihm geholfen hatte” — so the first participle stands bare. zum drittenmal is printed as one word here.

sentences.t: und so glaubte sie, er habe alles aus eigener Kunst gethan, und hatte Achtung vor ihm, denn sie dachte bei sich „der kann doch mehr als du!“
sentences.l: and so she believed he had done everything out of his own art, and had respect before him, for she thought to herself “he can do more than you after all!”
sentences.i: and so she believed he had done it all by his own skill, and she had respect for him, for she thought to herself: “He can do more than you!”
sentences.n: habe is the subjunctive of reported speech, marking what she believed rather than what was so. “Achtung vor jemandem haben” is to have respect for someone. She calls herself du in her own thoughts, which German does easily. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan. The tale closes on a marriage founded on something the husband never tells her.

glossary.bange: bange — afraid, anxious (es wird mir bange: I grow afraid, with the person in the dative)
glossary.ei: das Ei — egg (neut.; the same spelling is also the interjection ei, ‘well now’)
glossary.entdecke: entdecken — (she) discovers, detects, catches sight of (3rd sg. pres. subjunctive of reported speech)
glossary.entdeckte: entdecken — discovered, caught sight of (3rd sg. pret.)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun, and the impersonal subject of es war, es gieng)
glossary.fügte: sich fügen — submitted, yielded (3rd sg. pret.; sich seinem Schicksal fügen: to submit to one’s fate)
glossary.gefallen: das Gefallen — pleasure, liking (Gefallen an etwas haben: to take a liking to a thing)
glossary.grund: der Grund — the bottom, the floor (auf den Grund des Sees: to the bottom of the lake)
glossary.habs: habs = habe es — (I) have it (haben with the clitic es; ich habs heraus: I have got it, I have found it out)
glossary.herrschaft: die Herrschaft — rule, dominion, mastery (die Herrschaft behalten: to keep the rule to oneself)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, to it (dative of er and of es)
glossary.kehrte: heimkehren — turned homeward, went home (3rd sg. pret.; separable heim-)
glossary.korn: das Korn — the bead, the foresight on a gun barrel (jemanden aufs Korn nehmen: to draw a bead on, to take aim at)
glossary.krieche: kriechen — to creep, to crawl (here 3rd sg. pres. subjunctive in reported speech, and later the imperative krieche!, creep!)
glossary.laß: ablassen — leave off!, let be! (imperative laß … ab; separable ab-)
glossary.rath: rathen — advise!, counsel! (imperative sg.; 1857 spelling of rate, from raten — not the noun Rath, counsel)
glossary.reihe: die Reihe — row, line; nach der Reihe / der Reihe nach — in turn, one after another
glossary.sage: sagen — say!, tell! (imperative sg.; sage mir: tell me — not die Sage, a legend)
glossary.schieß: schießen — shoot! (imperative sg.; schieß nicht: do not shoot)
glossary.schweres: schwer — hard, difficult (neut. nom./acc. sg.; ein schweres Stück: a hard piece of work)
glossary.see: der See — lake (masc.; feminine die See is the sea, and only the article tells them apart)
glossary.tiefe: die Tiefe — the deep, the depths (fem. noun formed from tief)
glossary.todten: todt — dead (dat. pl. adj.; 1857 spelling of tot; mit todten Häuptern: with dead heads on them)
glossary.verloren: verlieren — lost (past part.; verloren sein: to be lost, to be done for)
glossary.versuche: versuchen — to try, to attempt (3rd sg. pres. subjunctive; wer es versuche: whoever should attempt it)
glossary.volk: das Volk — people, folk, a crowd (viel Volk: a great crowd)
glossary.werde: werden — will, shall (the future auxiliary; here 1st sg. ich werde, and 3rd sg. present subjunctive in reported speech)
glossary.zog: ziehen — moved, journeyed (3rd sg. pret.; in die Stadt ziehen: to go into the town)
